events.objective: Establish the symptom timeline and blast radius for the login failures. From ~06:00Z to 08:59Z, determine: (1) exact onset time of the auth-service p99 latency rise and 503s on /v1/auth/login; (2) whether the pattern is a sharp step change (regression-like) or a gradual trend (resource/leak-like); (3) error signatures in auth-service logs around onset (timeouts, connection refused, pool exhaustion, bcrypt-related messages, etc.); (4) whether only auth-service is affected or if other services show simultaneous latency/error anomalies, and whether any dependency (db, cache, session/token service) shows its own degradation starting at or before the auth onset. Report concrete timestamps and the services/endpoints involved.

Find what changed and when, across ALL services, in the window 2026-04-21T00:00Z to 2026-04-22T08:59Z. List all deployments and config changes with their timestamps and affected services, paying special attention to anything touching auth-service and its bcrypt/hashing path. Also map auth-service's dependency graph (what it calls and what calls it, and any shared components) so we can tell whether the fault could originate outside auth-service. Finally, search historical incidents for the prior bcrypt regression: what was the signature, root cause, and fix, so we can compare against the current signal.

args.query: connection pool exhausted timeouts shared database cache

events.statement: Across ALL services in 2026-04-21T00:00Z–2026-04-22T08:59Z there was exactly one deployment: portfolio-service v4.4.0 'Holdings export' (CSV export endpoint) at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z, status live, not rolled back.
No auth-service deployment occurred in the window, nor in the preceding three days (2026-04-18T00:00Z–2026-04-22T08:59Z): auth-service-scoped deployment count is 0.

The only config change across all services in the window is on auth-service: key log.level, INFO→WARN, at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z, described as 'Reduce log volume' — it does not touch bcrypt or the hashing/request path.

auth-service dependency graph: it calls user-db (kind db), redis-cache (kind cache) and kyc-provider (external); api-gateway calls auth-service (http). redis-cache is flagged shared=true, while user-db, auth-service and api-gateway are shared=false; kyc-provider has has_telemetry=false.

redis-cache is shared by four callers — auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service — so a fault originating in portfolio-service (which deployed at 05:50Z) could plausibly propagate to auth-service through that shared cache.

Historical precedent HIST-101 (2025-08-14, 'Login latency after auth-service release'): symptoms login p99 4s, 503 on login, high cpu; root cause 'bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0'; resolution 'Rolled back v6.4.0'. Its signature required a bad auth-service deployment — which is absent in the current window.

events.description: No metrics were queried in this round (budget spent on change history and dependency mapping), so I cannot state when auth-service latency/503s actually began, whether redis-cache or user-db show anomalies, or whether ~4s p99 correlates with auth-service CPU (the HIST-101 signature).

Deployment rollback status was only retrieved for the single in-window deployment (dep-5803, rolled_back_at null); no deployment history for services outside the queried window beyond auth-service was checked, and config-change history before 2026-04-21T00:00Z was not retrieved.
kyc-provider is an external dependency with has_telemetry=false; no data is available on its health or latency.

events.answer: In the full window 2026-04-21T00:00Z–2026-04-22T08:59Z there is exactly ONE deployment across all services — portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 2026-04-22T05:50Z — and ZERO auth-service deployments. The only config change is auth-service log.level INFO→WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40Z, which does not touch the hashing path. So the current signal differs from HIST-101's bcrypt regression, which was caused by a bad auth-service release (bcrypt cost 10→14) and fixed by rollback. auth-service depends on user-db (non-shared), redis-cache (SHARED with portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service) and external kyc-provider; api-gateway calls it. Because redis-cache is shared and portfolio-service deployed at 05:50Z, a shared-component path is plausible and cannot be ruled out from change history alone.

events.statement: auth-service p99 latency (latency_p99_ms) rises as a sharp STEP at the 06:52Z -> 06:54Z boundary: 91.5ms avg at 06:52Z, 93.94ms at 06:50Z, then 3759.86ms at 06:54Z, and remains ~3.6-3.9s through 08:54Z. Zoomed 120s buckets confirm the transition occurs within this single 2-minute bucket with no gradual ramp.
auth-service error_rate steps up in the same 06:48Z->06:54Z bucket: baseline ~0.19-0.27% through 06:48Z, then 11.72% at 06:54Z, sustained at ~13.7-14.4% through 08:54Z (max 15.67%).

The only ERROR signature in auth-service logs is queue saturation, not application/bcrypt errors: 372 ERROR entries, all matching "request rejected: accept queue full, returning <n> (POST /v<n>/auth/login)", first_seen 2026-04-22T06:55:42Z (returning 503), last 08:58:57Z.

auth-service request_rate steps up ~3.7x at the same 06:36Z->06:54Z bucket: ~393-442 req/s baseline (06:00-06:36Z) to 1452.66 req/s at 06:54Z, sustained ~1,490-1,510 req/s afterward, with a max of 1813.74. This coincides with the latency/error step.
auth-service CPU saturates at onset: ~37-38% (06:00-06:18Z), partial rise at 06:36Z (avg 44.66, max 96.96), then pinned at ~97% avg / ~98-99% max from 06:54Z through 08:42Z.

api-gateway shows the SAME sharp step at the 06:36Z->06:54Z bucket: p99 ~208-211ms baseline (06:00-06:36Z) -> 3908.96ms at 06:54Z, sustained ~3.87-3.94s through 08:42Z (max 4250.7ms). Impact propagates upstream of auth-service.

No bcrypt-related log messages exist in auth-service in the 06:50-08:59Z window: a WARN+ search for the term "bcrypt" returned total_matched=0 (searched data range 03:00-08:59Z). The report's bcrypt-regression hypothesis is not corroborated by any bcrypt log signature.

events.answer: The auth-service p99 latency and 503s on POST /v1/auth/login begin as a sharp step change between 06:52Z and 06:54Z (p99 ~90ms -> ~3,760ms, error_rate 0.2% -> ~11.7%, first "accept queue full" 503 log at 06:55:42Z), and stay flat/sustained for the next 2 hours. events.title: Traffic surge (3.7x login request rate) saturates auth-service CPU and its accept queue, not a code regression
Reporter's suspicion: bcrypt/hashing regression reintroduced in auth-service
portfolio-service v4.4.0 'Holdings export' floods the shared redis-cache, degrading auth-service transitively
Dependency (user-db / redis-cache / kyc-provider) slowdown is the true origin; auth-service is only where it surfaces

events.summary: H1 is the best-supported hypothesis: the 06:54Z step in latency, errors, CPU saturation and request_rate is verified (F7-F12), the only error signature is accept-queue-full (F9), and the alleged bcrypt regression is contradicted by the absence of any auth-service deployment (F2) and of bcrypt log messages (F13). However, two load-bearing hops are unverified and are exactly the discriminators between H1 and the live alternatives: (1) H1 assumes the 3.7x request-rate jump is genuine inbound demand, but the report never compared api-gateway inbound RPS to auth-service inbound RPS, so the surge could be a retry/duplicate artifact caused by an earlier dependency slowdown; (2) H4/H3 were never tested against telemetry because all dependency-metric queries were budget-exhausted. The onset is pinned only to a 2-minute bucket, so whether load precedes saturation is not shown. These are obtainable and could flip ranking, so confidence is capped at 0.5. Not inconclusive: decision-relevant data sources are available and queries remain.

events.objective: Compare api-gateway inbound request_rate to auth-service inbound request_rate over 06:30-07:00Z (sub-minute buckets if available). Determine whether api-gateway inbound RPS also jumped ~3.7x to ~1,500 req/s (genuine inbound demand) or stayed near baseline ~400 req/s while auth-service received ~1,500 req/s (surge is an internal retry/duplicate artifact). If any session/token/unique-login metric exists, report the ratio of auth-service request_rate to unique login sessions. Report concrete numbers and the gateway:auth RPS ratio across the onset.

For redis-cache, user-db and kyc-provider (where telemetry exists), report latency_p99, error_rate, and CPU/memory over 06:30-07:10Z. Did any rise at or before 06:52Z, i.e. BEFORE auth-service's step? Also report auth-service memory_pct trend over the same window. Explicitly state whether any dependency degrades first (supports H4/H3 dependency-origin) or only after (supports H1).

Test the shared-cache/co-caller path: report request_rate/throughput and error signatures (accept-queue-full, connection errors, timeouts) for portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service (all share redis-cache) during 06:30-07:00Z. Determine whether portfolio-service (deployed v4.4.0 at 05:50Z) shows elevated redis-cache traffic/rate AFTER its deploy, whether those co-callers show any simultaneous degradation near 06:52-06:54Z, and the exact quiet gap between the 05:50Z deploy and the 06:54Z onset. A ~1-hour quiet gap or absence of shared-cache anomalies in co-callers weakens the portfolio/shared-cache path; simultaneous failures in non-changed callers would point to shared infrastructure.

events.statement: api-gateway inbound request_rate rises in the same 06:50-07:00Z window as auth-service, on sub-minute (60s) buckets: ~1,244 req/s at 06:48Z -> 1,653 at 06:51Z -> 3,175 at 06:54Z -> 4,763 req/s at 07:00Z. It did NOT stay near ~400 req/s.
auth-service inbound request_rate on the same 60s buckets tracks the gateway: ~385 req/s at 06:48Z -> 1,012 at 06:54Z -> 1,814 at 06:59Z, i.e. both series move together rather than diverging.

The gateway:auth RPS ratio stays roughly constant across the onset: 06:30Z 1278.54/389.19 = 3.29; 06:54Z 3174.6/1012.36 = 3.14; 06:59Z 4859.74/1813.74 = 2.68. auth-service is not receiving ~3.7x the gateway's traffic; the gateway carries ~3x the auth-service load before, during and after onset.

Because the gateway's own inbound rate rose ~3.8x in parallel with auth-service's, the auth-service surge is externally-visible inbound demand, not a hidden internal retry/duplicate fan-out that would leave gateway inbound near baseline while auth-service spikes alone.

auth-service exposes no session/token/unique-login metric; its available_metrics are cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, rate_limited_per_min, request_rate, restarts. A request-to-unique-session ratio cannot be computed.

portfolio-service v4.4.0 ('Holdings export', CSV export endpoint, status live, rolled_back_at=null) was deployed at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z and is the only portfolio-service deployment in 2026-04-21T00:00Z–2026-04-22T08:59Z.

The quiet gap between the portfolio-service deploy (05:50Z) and the auth-service onset (06:54Z = first elevated bucket) is 64 minutes; there was no config change in 05:00–07:10Z to explain a trigger in between (config_changes count = 0 for all services).

Historical lead HIST-107 (2025-12-09, 'Cold cache storm after redis failover', services redis-cache + market-data-service) is a precedent for a shared redis-cache problem surfacing as downstream latency — but its root cause was a Redis primary failure/empty replica, a different mechanism from a single service flooding the cache. HIST-101 remains the only bcrypt precedent and it required a bad auth-service deploy, which is absent (F2).

events.answer: I could NOT directly measure the co-caller metric series: no portfolio-service, pricing-engine or market-data-service request_rate/throughput or error signatures were retrieved this round, and redis-cache has no latency/error metrics (per T4/F20). What I could confirm: portfolio-service v4.4.0 is the sole deployment (05:50Z) and the quiet gap to the 06:54Z onset is exactly 64 minutes; redis-cache and all co-callers are topologically linked only through the shared redis-cache. On the available evidence the shared-cache path stays untested by co-caller metrics, and no simultaneous co-caller degradation was observed because it was not measured — so H3 cannot be confirmed or refuted from my data, and the ~1-hour quiet gap after the 05:50Z deploy (with no rollback) is consistent with the team's finding that no dependency degrades before auth-service.

Reporter's suspicion: bcrypt/hashing regression reintroduced in auth-service

events.summary: H1 is now adequately supported and the viable alternatives are contradicted by measurement, not just argument. The causal chain rests on verified observations at every hop: a sharp step at the 06:52Z->06:54Z bucket in auth-service p99 (91ms->3.76s, F7), error_rate (0.2%->11.7%, F8), CPU (~38%->97%, F11), and request_rate (~400->1,452 req/s, F10), with request_rate also stepping on 60s buckets (F15); the gateway's own inbound RPS rises in parallel ~1,244->4,763 req/s (F14) with a stable gateway:auth ratio of 3.29/3.14/2.68 (F16), which refutes the retry-fan-out artifact my round-1 review flagged as the key discriminator; the only error signature is accept-queue-full (F9) with rate_limited_per_min stepping at the same boundary (F19); latency propagates upstream to api-gateway in the same bucket (F12); and memory is flat, excluding a leak (F25). The reported bcrypt regression is contradicted on three independent axes: zero auth-service deployments in-window and for three preceding days (F2), no request-path config change (F3), and zero bcrypt log matches (F13), while its historical precedent HIST-101 required a bad auth-service deploy (F6). The shared-redis paths (H3/H4) are contradicted by flat redis-cache CPU/memory with no pre-06:52Z rise (F21/F22), flat user-db CPU and slow queries (F23), a 64-minute quiet gap between the portfolio deploy and onset with no intervening change (F28), and no dependency degrading before auth-service (T4). Remaining uncertainty is in the unidentified traffic source and the unmeasurable kyc-provider path - it does not point to a different origin, so it justifies a confidence cap rather than "inconclusive". Notably, the team burned this round on change-history and topology queries while leaving the decisive load-vs-saturation ordering and per-client breakdown unqueried; further queries would refine the "why" (who sent the traffic), not change the "where" (auth-service capacity saturation), so I do not hold the incident open for them.

tasks.objective: Establish the symptom timeline and blast radius for the login failures. From ~06:00Z to 08:59Z, determine: (1) exact onset time of the auth-service p99 latency rise and 503s on /v1/auth/login; (2) whether the pattern is a sharp step change (regression-like) or a gradual trend (resource/leak-like); (3) error signatures in auth-service logs around onset (timeouts, connection refused, pool exhaustion, bcrypt-related messages, etc.); (4) whether only auth-service is affected or if other services show simultaneous latency/error anomalies, and whether any dependency (db, cache, session/token service) shows its own degradation starting at or before the auth onset. Report concrete timestamps and the services/endpoints involved.
tasks.answer: The auth-service p99 latency and 503s on POST /v1/auth/login begin as a sharp step change between 06:52Z and 06:54Z (p99 ~90ms -> ~3,760ms, error_rate 0.2% -> ~11.7%, first "accept queue full" 503 log at 06:55:42Z), and stay flat/sustained for the next 2 hours. The step is simultaneous with a ~3.7x jump in auth-service request_rate and CPU saturating at ~97%; api-gateway latency shows the same step at 06:54Z, so the impact propagates beyond auth-service. This pattern (step + CPU saturation + request surge) is not consistent with a gradual resource/leak trend and no bcrypt log messages were found.

critiques.summary: H1 is the best-supported hypothesis: the 06:54Z step in latency, errors, CPU saturation and request_rate is verified (F7-F12), the only error signature is accept-queue-full (F9), and the alleged bcrypt regression is contradicted by the absence of any auth-service deployment (F2) and of bcrypt log messages (F13). However, two load-bearing hops are unverified and are exactly the discriminators between H1 and the live alternatives: (1) H1 assumes the 3.7x request-rate jump is genuine inbound demand, but the report never compared api-gateway inbound RPS to auth-service inbound RPS, so the surge could be a retry/duplicate artifact caused by an earlier dependency slowdown; (2) H4/H3 were never tested against telemetry because all dependency-metric queries were budget-exhausted. The onset is pinned only to a 2-minute bucket, so whether load precedes saturation is not shown. These are obtainable and could flip ranking, so confidence is capped at 0.5. Not inconclusive: decision-relevant data sources are available and queries remain.

The claim that a shared-redis path is contradicted rests partly on timing, but the ~1-hour gap between the 05:50Z portfolio-service deploy and the 06:54Z onset, portfolio-service's redis load, and whether other shared-cache callers also fail, were never measured. critiques.summary: H1 is now adequately supported and the viable alternatives are contradicted by measurement, not just argument. The causal chain rests on verified observations at every hop: a sharp step at the 06:52Z->06:54Z bucket in auth-service p99 (91ms->3.76s, F7), error_rate (0.2%->11.7%, F8), CPU (~38%->97%, F11), and request_rate (~400->1,452 req/s, F10), with request_rate also stepping on 60s buckets (F15); the gateway's own inbound RPS rises in parallel ~1,244->4,763 req/s (F14) with a stable gateway:auth ratio of 3.29/3.14/2.68 (F16), which refutes the retry-fan-out artifact my round-1 review flagged as the key discriminator; the only error signature is accept-queue-full (F9) with rate_limited_per_min stepping at the same boundary (F19); latency propagates upstream to api-gateway in the same bucket (F12); and memory is flat, excluding a leak (F25). The reported bcrypt regression is contradicted on three independent axes: zero auth-service deployments in-window and for three preceding days (F2), no request-path config change (F3), and zero bcrypt log matches (F13), while its historical precedent HIST-101 required a bad auth-service deploy (F6). The shared-redis paths (H3/H4) are contradicted by flat redis-cache CPU/memory with no pre-06:52Z rise (F21/F22), flat user-db CPU and slow queries (F23), a 64-minute quiet gap between the portfolio deploy and onset with no intervening change (F28), and no dependency degrading before auth-service (T4). Remaining uncertainty is in the unidentified traffic source and the unmeasurable kyc-provider path - it does not point to a different origin, so it justifies a confidence cap rather than "inconclusive". Notably, the team burned this round on change-history and topology queries while leaving the decisive load-vs-saturation ordering and per-client breakdown unqueried; further queries would refine the "why" (who sent the traffic), not change the "where" (auth-service capacity saturation), so I do not hold the incident open for them.

challenges.issue: Origin of the surge is unresolved: gateway INFO+ logs for 06:45-07:05Z returned zero matches (GAPS), so no per-client/per-IP breakdown exists and auth-service has no session metric (F18). H1 therefore names auth-service as the constraint but cannot name the traffic source, and 'externally-driven' rests on an assumption rather than a positive identification of the caller.

Temporal ordering of load vs saturation is not established: onset is bounded only to a 2-minute bucket, and CPU shows a partial rise at 06:36Z (avg 44.66, max 96.96, F11) whose relationship to the request_rate rise (baselined 06:00-06:36Z) is unordered. Strictly, the chain asserts load->saturation without sub-minute proof that load precedes the queue overflow.

The kyc-provider branch is unfalsified because it has no telemetry (F24) and its caller-side signal was never queried, so 'no dependency degrades first' is not fully established for that path. However, even a kyc-provider fault could not produce a parallel 3.8x rise in BOTH gateway and auth inbound RPS (F14-F17), so this does not threaten H1's ranking.

The co-caller test was never actually run: portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service metrics for 06:30-07:00Z were not retrieved (T5/GAPS), so the shared-cache path is untested by the co-caller signal rather than contradicted by it. It is weakened by the 64-minute quiet gap (F28) and flat redis CPU/memory (F21/F22), but the decisive positive test is absent.

Rejection of the reporter's bcrypt hypothesis is sound but partly rests on absence-of-evidence: 'no deployment' (F2) is robust, but the bcrypt log search returned zero matches and the sole ERROR log query was truncated (30 of 372 lines, GAPS). The deployment absence alone is sufficient to reject H2, so this is not load-bearing.

Accept-queue-full plus ~97% CPU with a ~3.7x load increase does not by itself establish that ~1,500 req/s exceeds provisioned capacity at normal per-request cost - 'auth-service's provisioned capacity cannot absorb ~1,500 req/s' is an assumption in H1. No per-request cost or capacity-limit metric was pulled, so the margin between normal capacity and the surge is unquantified.
